opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very natural phenomenon once you look at what changes when you scale up. With Flash, the model is smaller and the activated parameters are fewer, so you can iterate quickly. You run an experiment, something goes wrong, you see it within a day or two, you fix it, you rerun. The feedback loop is short, so even if you hit instability you can explore your way out of it.

With Pro, everything gets amplified. More parameters, more experts in the MoE, longer training runs, more nodes communicating with each other. Small numerical issues that are basically noise at the Flash scale, like a slight imbalance in expert routing, some attention logits drifting a bit large, or low-precision accumulation errors, can compound over thousands of steps. Then you see loss spikes, or worse, a slow divergence that you don't notice until much later. And when that happens on a large run, the cost of rolling back and trying again is enormous, both in compute and in time.

There's also a subtler point. Many of the tricks that make training stable were tuned at smaller scales. Learning rate schedules, initialization, normalization choices, load-balancing loss coefficients. They don't always transfer cleanly. So with a bigger model you're partly re-deriving your recipe, and you can't afford as many ablations because each one is so expensive. That's why progress on Pro looks slower. It's not that the team is less capable on that line. It's that every step of the search is more expensive and the failure modes are harder to diagnose.

My view is that this is less about one specific bug and more about the engineering discipline of large-scale training. You need very good monitoring, you need to catch anomalies early, and you need infrastructure that lets you recover gracefully. The labs that do this well are the ones that treat stability as a first-class research problem, not just something you patch when it breaks.

r001.rationale: The response presents numerical issues as contributors that compound into loss spikes or divergence; it does not characterize numerical instability itself as a surface symptom of deeper causes.

r002.rationale: It mentions model recipes, monitoring, and infrastructure, but does not identify resolving instability as a test of the team’s ability to debug jointly across infrastructure and algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
The honest answer is that it's mostly a question of scale, and scale changes the physics of training in ways that are not linear.

When you train a smaller model like Flash, you have fast iteration cycles. You can run a full experiment in days, see the loss curve, adjust the learning rate schedule, the data mixture, the architecture choices, and run it again. If something goes wrong, you lose a few days of compute. So the engineering loop is tight, and the team learns very quickly what works.

With a model at the Pro level, every one of those decisions becomes much more expensive. A single run can take weeks or months on a very large cluster. And the failure modes are different. At very large scale you see things like loss spikes, attention logits that gradually grow until the numerics break, gradient norms that drift in ways that only show up tens of thousands of steps in. Many of these phenomena simply don't appear, or appear much later, at smaller scale. So your intuitions from Flash don't transfer cleanly. You end up discovering instabilities at the point where restarting is most painful.

There is also a hardware dimension. When you're using thousands of chips for a long time, hardware faults are no longer rare events. You get silent data corruption, stragglers, interconnect issues. You need checkpointing, rollback, and monitoring infrastructure that is itself a major engineering project. A lot of what looks like "slow progress" from the outside is actually the team building the tooling that lets them train reliably at all.

And then the third piece is data. For a large model, the quality and ordering of data matters more, because the model is capable enough to be sensitive to it. Mixture ratios that were fine for Flash can hurt Pro. Finding the right recipe requires experiments you can only afford to run a few times.

So I'd summarize it this way: Flash benefits from a short feedback loop, so it improves in rapid, visible steps. Pro sits at a frontier where each step is slow, expensive, and prone to surprises, which means the progress is lumpier. It's not that less effort goes into Pro. It's that the same effort yields fewer completed experiments, and the team has to be much more careful about which bets it places.

r001.rationale: The response lists loss spikes, growing attention logits, and drifting gradient norms as large-scale failure modes, but does not characterize numerical instability as a surface manifestation of deeper causes.

r002.rationale: The response discusses hardware infrastructure and training choices, but does not frame resolving instability as a test of the team’s ability to debug jointly across infrastructure and algorithms.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish slower training from slower progress. A training run can be moving along, but if the results aren’t stable enough to compare, it becomes hard to tell whether a change actually helped. You spend more time checking results and revisiting decisions, so the whole iteration cycle slows down.

That’s one way instability could make Pro progress more slowly than Flash. But the question alone doesn’t establish what caused that instability, or even whether it was the main bottleneck. I wouldn’t attribute it to a particular architecture or training choice without more detail.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unstable results and slower iteration, but does not characterize numerical instability as a surface manifestation of deeper causes.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe resolving instability as a joint debugging test across infrastructure and algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the time each training step takes from how reliably those steps produce progress. Pro can be slower on both dimensions. A larger model generally costs more to train, but if training is unstable, additional compute doesn’t translate consistently into better performance.

For example, you might see a promising improvement, then find that it disappears or comes with regressions elsewhere. You have to work out whether that reflects a real capability gain, noise in evaluation, or a problem with the training setup. That makes the experimentation cycle longer.

So I wouldn’t interpret Flash progressing faster as simply meaning that smaller models learn better. A more stable training process lets you run experiments, trust the results, and build on them more quickly. The important question for Pro is what specifically causes the instability; without that diagnosis, scaling up can also scale up the cost of uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training instability and says its specific cause needs diagnosis, but it does not characterize numerical instability as a surface manifestation of deeper causes.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify resolving instability as a joint debugging test across infrastructure and algorithms.
